claim: When a boolean cut against a curved cutter (e.g. a sphere sunk into a cube edge) is genuinely needed, don't apply the boolean to the production mesh. Duplicate the target into three copies (renamed here 'final cube', 'patch', 'sphere'), apply the Boolean modifier only to the disposable 'patch' copy against the cutter, then immediately hide the cutter. The raw boolean output is never treated as finished geometry -- it is used only as a scratch reference to capture the exact intersection profile, then heavily manually rebuilt (n-gon cleanup, re-inset, boundary straightening) before being grafted back into the real model.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript, framing at ~26s: 'there's only one tool we can use to create this cut and that is the boolean modifier, i don't use it often but it does have its uses and this is one of them but we'll use light geometry for the cutout object and virtually no geometry at all for the area that's being cut, the cleanup will be minimal.' At ~81-97s three duplicated cubes are renamed 'final cube' ('this will be the final subdivision surface model but we need to do a few other things first'), 'patch', and 'sphere'. At ~158-171s the Boolean modifier is added to the patch object only, targeting the sphere: 'i'm going to apply this modifier straight away and hide the sphere to see what we've got.' The closing line at ~1059s reinforces the same pattern: 'this is one of the main methods i use when i'm given boolean sketches of objects and i start remaking them properly.'
rejected_alternative: Applying the Boolean modifier directly to the actual production mesh and treating its output as final geometry -- the approach this project's own prior research (the Connecting Cylinders video, captured separately) found 'destroys topology instantly with zero chance of recovery.'
reason: This is the direct answer to whether this video contradicts this project's existing 'never trust raw boolean output' stance: it does not contradict it, it agrees with it. The boolean here is explicitly a disposable measurement/reference step on a throwaway duplicate, immediately discarded in favor of manually rebuilt topology -- not a demonstration that boolean output itself is safe to keep. The actionable distinction for this project's boolean-workflow gap is boolean-as-scratch-tool versus boolean-as-final-geometry.

claim: After a boolean cut leaves n-gons and stray vertices along the cut boundary, exploit the fact that the boolean's own defect vertices typically have exactly two edges each: in Edit Mode select any one such vertex, then Select > Select Similar > Amount of Connecting Edges to select every vertex sharing that same low edge count across the whole mesh, then X > Dissolve Vertices to remove them all in one pass, collapsing the surrounding n-gons back into clean topology.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript: 'if i tap into edit mode here we'll see a lot of problems there are a lot of n-gons and a lot of stray vertices and that's the nature of the boolean modifier that's what it does... on the inside of our cut we do have n-gons all over the place and that's not acceptable but the fix is really very simple all of the problem vertices have only two edges coming out of them and we can use that to our advantage... select similar and amount of connecting edges and now we can see that all of those vertices all around the edge have been selected so we can just press x and choose dissolve vertices and they're gone and now the inside of our cut has a really good topology' (~171-226s). Two large, badly-n-gon'd faces are explicitly not fixed this way -- per the narration they are simply deleted later since they fall outside the kept patch area.
rejected_alternative: Manually selecting and dissolving each stray boolean vertex one at a time, or manually rebuilding the n-gons edge-by-edge.
reason: A reusable, near-zero-cost cleanup rule for this project's own boolean-workflow gap (no post-boolean cleanup step currently exists): a large class of boolean n-gon damage collapses to a one-click Select Similar + Dissolve Vertices pass, provided the cutter geometry was kept light enough that the defect vertices are genuinely low-valence.

claim: To make a boolean-cut patch reusable as a clean insertable piece: select all faces on the patch's outer boundary (invert-selecting from the known interior loop is one fast way), Inset once, then Inset again with 'Edge Rail' enabled in the operator options so the second inset follows existing edge directions instead of drifting to odd angles, then delete the now-redundant outer ring of faces, leaving a clean two-loop-wide connection border. Because that border is not yet planar/axis-aligned, straighten each side by hand: select the inner and outer boundary vertices along one edge run, set the transform pivot to Active Element, make one boundary vertex the active element (shift-click it twice), then scale-constrain that whole run to 0 along whichever local axis that edge run should be flat on (S, X/Y/Z, 0) -- repeated per side and corner of the patch.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript: the Edge Rail step at ~285-293s ('we need to go down to the inside faces property box and turn on edge rail and this forces the inset to follow any existing edges'); then at ~326-333s 'this patch is an awkward shape to connect to anything so we need to fix that first and that's why we performed the second of the insets'; then the straightening routine repeated per side through ~466s, e.g. 'if i change the transform pivot point to active element... shift and click this vertex twice and it'll turn white meaning it's the active element in the selection if i now press s to scale y to constrain it to the y axis and type 0 those will all be straightened up along the y axis.'
rejected_alternative: Leaving the boolean-cleaned patch boundary at whatever irregular angles the inset left it, then attempting to snap/merge it onto a target mesh anyway, which the narration implies would leave stray-angle seams.
reason: This project has no existing technique for turning a cleaned boolean fragment into a reusable insert piece; the Edge-Rail-inset plus active-element-scale-to-zero straightening is a concrete, repeatable way to force an irregular patch boundary flat/axis-aligned before it needs to snap onto another mesh.

claim: To graft a cleaned boolean patch back into the production mesh: enable vertex snapping, then on the target mesh add loop cuts (Ctrl+R, typing an exact count where needed) positioned to snap onto the patch's boundary vertices one at a time (slide with G, letting snapping lock each loop/vertex into place), delete the target-mesh faces now covered by the patch, then join the objects (Ctrl+J) and run Merge by Distance. Before merging, count the patch boundary's vertices (e.g. Alt-click the loop and read the vertex count in the header) to know the exact number of merges expected; after Merge by Distance, check the reported number of removed vertices against that expected count and nudge the merge distance up or down until it matches exactly, rather than trusting the default distance to have welded the seam correctly.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript: 'now we need to add some loops to our shape to match the connection area for the patch... i'm going to turn on snapping and make it vertex snapping' (~479-489s), loop-cut-and-slide-to-snap repeated across ~497-570s; 'i'm going to alt click on the outside loop just because i need to know how many vertices it contains and i can see down here that it's made up of 24 vertices' (~609-617s); 'press ctrl and j to join... let's get rid of the overlapping vertices... press m and choose buy distance and we can see down here that it's got rid of 22 vertices and we need that to be 24 so if i just nudge up the merge distance by one click that'll normally do the trick and that changes it to 24 vertices that's what we need' (~625-654s).
rejected_alternative: Running Merge by Distance at its default threshold and assuming the seam is fully welded, without checking the resulting vertex count against the known boundary vertex count -- which could silently leave duplicate/unwelded vertices or over-merge nearby geometry.
reason: A verification habit this project's boolean/join workflow currently lacks: treating 'merge by distance ran' as insufficient proof of a clean weld, and instead checking the actual before/after vertex-count delta against a known expected number.

claim: Even after a boolean-derived patch has been fully cleaned to good quad topology and subdivided, a boolean-origin 3-spoke pole can still leave a subtle light-pinching artifact under Subdivision Surface -- visible per the narration as a highlight that changes size as the camera orbits past that pole, and confirmable more precisely by switching to a zebra-stripe MatCap, where the stripes visibly bend inward toward the pole instead of running straight. This is presented as a distinct symptom from the previously known UV-sphere pole-pinch problem, and clean quad topology alone does not resolve it -- it requires a separate vertex-position correction.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript: 'there's still one unresolved problem if i switch to the red madcap we'll see that as we orbit the camera around we can see that this point of light gets smaller at a certain point and then larger as we orbit the camera around... that's happening around this three sparked pole it gets bigger and then it gets smaller... the light is being pinched in towards the three spark pole because it's in the wrong place... if i switch to the zebra stripe mad cap we can take a closer look at what's happening now you see these lines are bending in towards the three-spark pole' (~707-747s).
rejected_alternative: Treating clean quad topology plus a Subdivision Surface modifier as sufficient proof the model is shading-clean, without checking the final result under a matcap/zebra-stripe material for pole-pinch artifacts.
reason: A concrete diagnostic step this project's own review passes should add after any boolean-cleanup or pole-heavy construction: checking for orbit-dependent highlight pinching near 3/5-spoke poles under a zebra-stripe matcap, not just checking topology cleanliness.

claim: To fix vertex-position-caused light pinching around an extraordinary pole on a curved surface (as opposed to a topology problem): select the affected vertices around the pole, Ctrl+G to make them a named vertex group; add a Laplacian Smooth modifier, move it above/before the Subdivision Surface modifier in the stack (temporarily disabling Subsurf first, since Laplacian Smooth can be slow to process through subdivided geometry), set the modifier's vertex group to the one just created so it only affects the problem area, then increase the Repeat value while watching the surface in Edit Mode with 'On Cage' enabled -- the value goes up to 200 but a much lower value (around 130, tuned by eye until the bent lines straighten) was enough here -- then apply the modifier and re-enable Subsurf.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript: 'what we need to do is change the position of these vertices but that's too difficult to do by hand we're going to use a modifier to do it for us... press control and g to make those a vertex group and i'm going to rename that to pinch fix... the modifier we're going to use is called the smooth laplacian, it's purpose is to recalculate the position of extraordinary vertices on a curved surface... we need to turn off the subdivision surface modifier... i'll choose smooth laplacian and then i'll move that to the top of the stack and i can turn our subdivision surface modifier back on... i'll choose the pinch fix vertex group... as i increase the repeat value you'll see that these lines start to straighten out... it goes all the way up to 200 but that's a little too much i normally set it to around 130' (~751-851s).
rejected_alternative: Per the video's own framing, dismissing Laplacian Smooth as just a (confusingly named, apparently useless) smoothing tool, or trying to nudge the pinched vertices by hand ('that's too difficult to do by hand').
reason: A previously-uncaptured, narrowly-scoped modifier technique (vertex-group-limited Laplacian Smooth, placed before Subsurf) for correcting real vertex-position defects on curved surfaces -- directly usable as the follow-up fix any time the VISUAL_CUE item above is triggered during a review pass.

claim: When a boolean cut against a curved cutter is unavoidable, deliberately keep the cutter object's own geometry as low-resolution as possible before applying the boolean -- e.g. build the cutter sphere from a cube with only one Subdivision Surface level applied, then cast it to a sphere with To Sphere, rather than a dense UV Sphere or a highly-subdivided mesh. Boolean n-gon/stray-vertex damage scales with the cutter's face count, so a deliberately light cutter keeps the resulting cleanup small and predictable.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript: 'now to make the sphere i'm just going to press ctrl and 2 to add a subdivision surface modifier... apply the subdivision surface modifier... because this is the actual geometry we'll use now as you know it's ball like but it's not quite a sphere' (~99-118s), and the explicit payoff later: 'because we cut quite a light geometry from only two phases the cleanup will be really simple' (~179-184s).
rejected_alternative: Using a dense, high-poly UV Sphere or other high-resolution mesh as the boolean cutter for precision, which by the video's own stated logic would multiply the stray n-gon vertices left behind and make the Select-Similar cleanup trick far less contained.
reason: A cheap, proactive rule for the rare cases this project does reach for a boolean: the cutter's own resolution is a direct lever on how much cleanup a boolean creates, and should be minimized deliberately rather than left at whatever a primitive defaults to.

claim: The Subdivision Surface modifier should always be positioned as the very last modifier in the stack; other deforming modifiers placed after it (the video's example: three Wave modifiers driving an unrelated animated bonus object) will not act correctly on the subdivided surface and should be moved above it.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript: 'i need to put the subdivision surface modifier at the end of the stack and that'll do a much better job the subdivision surface modifier should always be the very last thing in a stack' (~1023-1032s), said while fixing an unrelated animated bonus object, not the main boolean-cut model.
rejected_alternative: Leaving Subdivision Surface in the middle of a modifier stack and adding further deforming modifiers after it, expecting them to still act on the final subdivided shape.
reason: General modifier-ordering hygiene stated explicitly and in passing; low novelty but cheap to note as an explicit, sourced rule for this project's own modifier stacks rather than assumed convention.
